newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew gather strength before tricky docking.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew gather strength before tricky docking.

text.p: The Russian-U.S. crew aboard the crippled Mir station had some good news on Sunday after the worst trouble in its 11-year history.

A mission control expert told Reuters the station's navigation problem had been fixed and its gyrodines -- the devices that keep its solar panels lined up to the Sun to gain maximum power -- were now working.
"Yesterday evening all 12 gyrodines have been put into motion and they now work in a stable manner," the expert, who declined to be named, said by telephone.

An official dealing with links with the cosmonauts said later that the crew had spent the day gathering strength for the Monday morning docking of a supply ship which will bring equipment to help them fix the station's damaged power supply.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, engineer Alexander Lazutkin and British-born American Michael Foale had spent the day exercising and resting and had all spoken to their families.
"Mission control transmitted their favourite music to the Mir space station," said the official, who declined to be named.
"In the latest radio exchange 20 minutes ago the cosmonauts said they felt fine. Their blood pressures and temperatures are normal and they are in a good mood," he added.
He said that in the last radio exchange doctors would ask the crew to go to bed. "They need to sleep well before tomorrow's hard day," he said.
The official said the docking of the supply ship, expected at 0959 Moscow time on Monday (0559 gmt) was on target. "All its systems are working normally and it's ready for docking."
The expert had said earlier that a problem with a solar battery panel on the Progress cargo craft, launched on Saturday from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, had been overcome.
"It unfolded fully today and the ship is getting 100 percent energy," he said.

The supplies aboard the unmanned Progress M-35 include oxygen, food and water as well as repair tools. Experts say the overall lack of power on Mir will make the docking operation for Progress problematic.
The station lost up to half its power on June 25 after a collision with an unmanned cargo craft punctured the Spektr scientific module and cut off supplies from some panels.
It was the worst accident since Mir was first blasted into its orbit around the Earth more than 11 years ago.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov said on Thursday there had also been an unexplained malfunction in all of the station's gyrodines. The result was that the cosmonauts had to fire their rocket engines to keep Mir lined up to the Sun and prevent a further loss of electrical power.
The specialist did not say how the devices had been repaired and who -- mission control by remote commands or the crew -- had carried out the repairs.

The good news on the gyrodines followed another bout of trouble which happened on Tuesday but was disclosed only on Saturday when Russian and NASA officials confirmed that there had been a mystery leak from the holed Spektr module.

A Russian specialist said: "Five days ago, in one of our communications with the crew, we were told they had seen flakes and bubbles from an unknown source leaking from the Spektr module." He added it was not fuel.
The leak had been into space rather than inside, and there had been no repeat since that single incident.

"We are very concerned about what was in that module, what might have ruptured, and what the impact might be on the suited crew members," veteran astronaut Frank Culbertson, who runs NASA's missions to Mir, told a news conference.

It highlighted the dangers facing the crew during a sortie to Spektr on July 17 or 18 when Tsibliev and Lazutkin plan to enter the crippled module in their space suits to reconnect electrical cables and restore some power lost after the crash.
Michael Foale is to sit out the repair inside the station's emergency escape ship.
